entries.what_happened: Two manuscripts, both titled as counterexamples to Ryser's covering conjecture, claim the conjecture is false at infinitely many ranks. (1) 'Balanced counterexamples to Ryser's conjecture at prime orders' (dated 27 September 2026): for every sufficiently large prime q it constructs a finite intersecting (q+1)-partite (q+1)-uniform hypergraph H with covering number τ(H) = q+1, with exactly q+1 nonisolated vertices in each part. Since ν(H) = 1, this gives τ(H) = r > (r−1)ν(H) at r = q+1. The construction starts from the affine plane over F_q, with one vertex part per direction and one vertex per line. In each direction it merges two lines into one block and splits two other lines into two blocks each, so the count is (q−4)+1+4 = q+1. Each split line keeps four designated points, split into opposite pairs. The split lines are chosen by a probabilistic argument (random constituent lines, candidate four-point tuples, an independent-transversal selection, and a local-lemma completion). Covers of size at most q are excluded by a deletion estimate that gives an almost-cover, followed by the Szőnyi–Weiner prime-plane stability theorem to force a large pencil; this is the only step where primality of q is used. The paper also derives a corollary: a complete graph with a (q+1)-edge-coloring whose vertices need exactly q+1 monochromatic trees to cover, and the same minimum for connected monochromatic subgraphs. (2) 'A counterexample to Ryser's covering conjecture' (dated 23 September 2026): for every prime s ≥ s₀ with s ≡ 2 (mod 3), and every odd n ≥ n₀(s), with q = s^n, it constructs an intersecting (q+1)-partite (q+1)-uniform hypergraph H with τ(H) = q+1, so r = s^n+1. The paper does not assert equal part sizes. The construction takes the prime plane F_s², removes one line of each nonzero finite slope to get a set Y, and applies the bijection f(x,y) = (x³,y) (bijective because s ≡ 2 mod 3). A gadget lemma then says any cover of f(Y) by a lines and b points with a + b/2 ≤ s must be a full parallel class. Copies of Y are embedded in F_{s^n} with exceptional edges that change labels in one or two directions, using independent random candidate translates and an independent-transversal selection. The ambient cover argument uses an incidence bound proved in the paper along the sum–product strategy of Bourgain–Katz–Tao, valid when every proper subfield of F_q has order at most q^{1/3}; for odd n every proper subfield has order at most s^{n/3} = q^{1/3}. The paper also derives an r-edge-coloring corollary with r = s^n+1 that needs r monochromatic trees (or connected monochromatic subgraphs, or maximal components) to cover, which refutes Gyárfás's monochromatic tree-cover conjecture at these ranks, along with the Miličević bounded-diameter strengthening and the α = 1 case of a DeBiasio–Kamel–McCourt–Sheats conjecture, as the companion states.
entries.delivers: Refutes Ryser's conjecture in the form the problem states: for every r ≥ 2 and every r-partite r-uniform hypergraph H, τ(H) ≤ (r−1)ν(H). Both manuscripts state exactly this inequality as their eq:ryser, so the r-partite reading matches. Each counterexample is intersecting, so ν(H) = 1 and τ(H) = r exceeds (r−1)ν(H) at that rank. Ranks covered: (1) balanced paper: r = q+1 for every prime q ≥ q₀, with q₀ existential. (2) companion paper: r = s^n+1 for every prime s ≡ 2 (mod 3) with s ≥ s₀ and every odd n ≥ n₀(s), with s₀ and n₀(s) existential. Both families of ranks are infinite, so the universal claim (for every r) is refuted, and so is the inequality at each covered r. The matching-number part of the problem is refuted only at ν = 1, which is enough for the refutation. The balanced paper also gives equal part sizes |V₁| = … = |V_{q+1}| = q+1 with τ(H) = q+1; this is a stronger property than the problem requires. The companion does not assert balance and says so.
entries.remains: If the claims are correct, the conjecture as stated fails and nothing of the universal form survives. What these manuscripts leave open: (a) the inequality at every rank r not of the form q+1 (q prime ≥ q₀) or s^n+1 (in the companion's range), including the small ranks where the manuscripts cite positive results (the intersecting case through rank four attributed to Gyárfás, rank five to Tuza, and linear hypergraphs through rank nine); (b) the inequality for hypergraphs with ν ≥ 2, which the manuscripts do not treat directly; (c) the exact set of covered ranks, since the thresholds q₀, s₀ and n₀(s) are not quantified; (d) any sharp form of the bound in terms of r.
entries.direction: disproves the conjecture at infinitely many ranks (intersecting counterexamples)
entries.object: Yes, but not explicit. For each large prime q, an intersecting (q+1)-partite (q+1)-uniform hypergraph H with τ(H) = q+1 and parts of size q+1 (balanced paper). For each s ≡ 2 (mod 3) and odd n in the companion's range, an intersecting (s^n+1)-partite (s^n+1)-uniform hypergraph H with τ(H) = s^n+1 (companion paper). Each H is defined from a configuration whose existence is shown by a probabilistic argument with positive or high probability, with no numerical threshold, so no closed-form construction is given.
entries.conditional_on: Balanced paper: no unproven hypothesis. It uses the Szőnyi–Weiner prime-plane stability theorem (Szőnyi–Weiner 2012, Theorem 4; also Héger–Nagy, Result 3.6) as an external black box, in the form the paper restates with explicit constants. It also uses the Lovász local lemma and an Azuma-type bound; the latter is proved in its appendix. Companion paper: no unproven hypothesis in the statements. It takes three elementary estimates (affine second-moment identity, bounded-drift concentration, and the independent-trial exposure bound) from the appendix of the balanced paper, which it cites as Lemmas A.1–A.3; I checked the appendix statements and proofs of A.1 and A.2. It follows the Bourgain–Katz–Tao sum–product strategy for its incidence theorem and proves the incidence theorem itself, and it proves its own Freedman-type martingale bound.
entries.doubts: Neither manuscript gives a numerical threshold; both say so. The balanced paper says its threshold 'is not numerical' and rests on finitely many 'with probability o(1)' estimates, combined by subtracting failure probabilities from a positive lower bound. Its deletion theorem covers any probability law that is at most e^{Kq} times uniform. The text says a qualitative estimate for uniform deletion would not suffice under this change of measure, and the introduction attributes the needed saving to a profile-counting bound of order exp(−Ω(q log q)); that step is carried out in deletion.tex. Several arguments are closed by 'as before' or 'the same process as before' (candidates.tex, selection.tex). The companion's gadget lemma and pool lemma hold only with high probability as s or n tend to infinity, and their constants δ = exp(−4K(s−1)) and ρ = δ/10 depend on s, so its thresholds depend on s through these constants. No inconsistency between the abstracts and the main theorems of either paper was found. I did not check the long probabilistic estimates line by line; this entry reports what the text claims and how it is organized.
